Terminaison présynaptique de notre axone: Presynaptic terminal of our axon: ≈ 200 synaptic vesicles, about ten of them docked at the active zone, facing the spine of a neighbouring neuron. Enter it through the clathrin-coated pit, or approach the cleft from outside: the ship shrinks until it can slip in. Every molecule of the synapse has its own card. The ⚡ button lets you follow a nerve impulse from end to end.
Tête de ≈ 0,5 µm portée par un col étroi: A head of ≈ 0.5 µm on a narrow neck; its membrane hugs our bouton at a distance of 20 nm. Beneath that membrane lies the postsynaptic density: AMPA and NMDA receptors, then the layered scaffold of PSD-95, GKAP, Shank and Homer, linked to actin. Inserting or removing AMPA receptors underlies long-term potentiation and depression.
Une des ≈ 10 000 épines de notre neurone: One of the ≈ 10,000 spines of our neuron, with its excitatory synapse. Its narrow neck (≈ 0.1 to 0.2 µm) makes it a biochemical compartment: Ca²⁺ entering through NMDA receptors stays confined there, which makes plasticity specific to each synapse. This is where the ⚡ nerve-impulse tour begins.
Renflement « en passant » d'un axone ven: An “en passant” swelling of an axon coming from another neuron. A hippocampal bouton has on average one active zone of ≈ 0.04 µm², about ten docked vesicles and ≈ 200 vesicles in all (Schikorski and Stevens 1997). An action potential releases a vesicle there only with a certain probability.
Collatérale fine et sans myéline d'un ne: A thin, unmyelinated collateral of an upstream neuron. It forms an “en passant” bouton every few micrometres and so contacts thousands of neurons.
≈ 20 nm séparent les deux membranes, soi: ≈ 20 nm separate the two membranes, about five membrane thicknesses. The cleft is spanned by adhesion molecules (neurexins, neuroligins, cadherins) that keep the two sides aligned. Released glutamate reaches ≈ 1 mM there and is gone within ≈ 1 ms (Clements 1992): diffusion, then uptake by astrocyte transporters.
Trimère de la membrane astrocytaire (gèn: A trimer of the astrocyte membrane (gene SLC1A2), present in thousands of copies per µm². It brings in one glutamate with 3 Na⁺ and 1 H⁺ and exports 1 K⁺: enough to keep extracellular glutamate below one micromolar. In the astrocyte, glutamine synthetase converts glutamate into glutamine (the glutamate–glutamine cycle).
Vésicule de ≈ 40 nm retenue contre la zo: A ≈ 40 nm vesicle held against the active zone, its SNARE complexes half zippered: it is ready to fuse as soon as Ca²⁺ arrives. An active zone holds about ten of them (the readily releasable pool). Docking and priming depend on RIM, Munc13-1 and Munc18-1.
Faisceau de quatre hélices long de ≈ 12: A bundle of four helices ≈ 12 nm long: syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 (two helices) on the plasma membrane, synaptobrevin-2 (VAMP2) on the vesicle. Its zippering, from the N-terminal end towards the membranes, forces them together and supplies the energy for fusion. NSF and α-SNAP then take it apart using ATP. Botulinum and tetanus toxins are proteases that cleave these three proteins.
Petite hélice fixée dans le sillon du co: A small helix lodged in the groove of the half-zippered SNARE complex. It stabilises the complex while holding fusion back; Ca²⁺-bound synaptotagmin releases this brake.
The Ca²⁺ sensor of fast release. Anchored in the vesicle, it carries two C2 domains (C2A binds 3 Ca²⁺, C2B binds 2) which, once loaded, plunge into the phospholipids of the plasma membrane and trigger fusion in less than a millisecond. Its low affinity (tens of µM) restricts fusion to vesicles sitting right next to an open calcium channel.
A protein of the SM family (gene STXBP1). It holds syntaxin-1 folded, then guides assembly of the SNARE complex; without it there is no neurotransmitter release. STXBP1 variants cause a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
Longue protéine (≈ 20 nm) dressée entre: A long protein (≈ 20 nm) standing between the vesicle and the plasma membrane. Its MUN domain opens syntaxin-1: this is the priming step. Its C1 and C2 domains make it sensitive to diacylglycerol and Ca²⁺, hence short-term plasticity.
The central organiser of the active zone. It binds Rab3 on the vesicle and Munc13-1, and tethers Cav2 channels through its PDZ domain, with the help of RIM-BP. Its nanoclusters mark the release sites, aligned across the cleft with the nanodomains of AMPA receptors: the “nanocolumn” (Tang 2016).
Protéine de liaison de RIM. Ses domaines: RIM-binding protein. Its SH3 domains attach Cav2 channels to RIM and keep them within a few tens of nanometres of the docked vesicles.
Canal Ca²⁺ dépendant du voltage ; sa sou: A voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel; its α1A subunit is encoded by CACNA1A (episodic ataxia type 2, familial hemiplegic migraine type 1, SCA6). Opened by the action potential, it creates around itself a nanodomain where Ca²⁺ reaches tens of µM for less than a millisecond. Release varies as roughly the 4th power of Ca²⁺.
Pompe à protons rotative : elle acidifie: A rotary proton pump: it acidifies the vesicle (pH ≈ 5.6) at the expense of ATP. One or two per vesicle are enough. The gradient it creates drives glutamate loading.
Transporteur vésiculaire du glutamate (≈: Vesicular glutamate transporter (≈ 10 per vesicle). It uses the electrochemical proton gradient, mainly its electrical component, to concentrate glutamate to more than 100 mM inside the vesicle.
Deux protéines géantes (≈ 420 et ≈ 550 k: Two giant proteins (≈ 420 and ≈ 550 kDa) stretched as filaments from the active zone into the bouton. They guide vesicles towards the release sites and organise the cytomatrix.
Échafaudage de la zone active. Avec RIM,: Scaffold of the active zone. Together with RIM, these proteins assemble the cytomatrix and recruit calcium channels and vesicles to it.
Elles relient les vésicules de réserve e: They link reserve vesicles to one another and to actin. During activity, their phosphorylation (CaMKII, PKA) frees vesicles, which move to the active zone.
Autour de la zone active, la membrane de: Around the active zone, the membrane of fused vesicles is retrieved: AP-2 and clathrin curve the membrane in about ten seconds. An ultrafast pathway (≈ 50 to 100 ms) also exists. The regenerated vesicles are re-acidified, then refilled with glutamate.
GTPase qui s'enroule en collier autour d: A GTPase that wraps as a collar around the neck of the pit and severs it. DNM1 variants cause a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
Molécules d'adhérence présynaptiques (NR: Presynaptic adhesion molecules (NRXN1 to NRXN3). Alternative promoters and splicing produce thousands of isoforms, a kind of identity code for synapses. They bind neuroligins, LRRTMs and cerebellins. NRXN1 deletions predispose to autism and schizophrenia.
Partenaires postsynaptiques des neurexin: Postsynaptic partners of neurexins, as dimers: NLGN1 at excitatory synapses, NLGN2 at inhibitory synapses. Their tail binds PSD-95. Variants of NLGN3 and NLGN4X are associated with autism.
Adhérence homophile dépendante du Ca²⁺,: Ca²⁺-dependent homophilic adhesion at the periphery of the synapse. Linked to actin through catenins, it stabilises the spine.
Canal cationique tétramérique (GluA1 à G: A tetrameric cation channel (GluA1 to GluA4, genes GRIA1 to GRIA4) opened by glutamate in less than a millisecond: Na⁺ flows in, giving the fast excitatory current. Low affinity: only receptors facing the release site open, hence their clustering in nanodomains. The edited GluA2 subunit (Q/R) makes the channel impermeable to Ca²⁺. A few tens to about a hundred per synapse; their number sets the strength of the synapse.
Sous-unités auxiliaires des récepteurs A: Auxiliary subunits of AMPA receptors. Their tail binds PSD-95, which holds the receptors in the postsynaptic density; they also modulate channel gating. γ-8 predominates in the hippocampus.
Tétramère de 2 GluN1 et 2 GluN2 (GRIN1,: A tetramer of 2 GluN1 and 2 GluN2 (GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B). Three conditions for it to conduct: glutamate, a co-agonist (glycine or D-serine) and depolarisation, which expels the Mg²⁺ plugging the pore. Slow and highly permeable to Ca²⁺, it detects the coincidence of pre- and postsynaptic activity and triggers plasticity. Variants of the GRIN genes cause neurodevelopmental disorders and epilepsies.
Récepteur couplé à Gq, en dimère, en cou: A Gq-coupled receptor, dimeric, forming a ring around the postsynaptic density. It activates phospholipase C (IP3, diacylglycerol) and modulates plasticity. Homer links it to Shank and to IP3 receptors.
Protéine d'échafaudage majeure (gène DLG: The major scaffold protein (gene DLG4): three PDZ domains, an SH3 and a GK; ≈ 300 copies per synapse. Palmitoylated and standing upright beneath the membrane, it holds NMDA receptors (GluN2 tail) and AMPA receptors (through TARPs). Its most abundant partner is SynGAP (SYNGAP1). Variants of DLG4 and SYNGAP1 cause intellectual disability.
Protéines DLGAP1 à DLGAP4 : elles relien: Proteins DLGAP1 to DLGAP4: they link the GK domain of PSD-95 to Shank, between the superficial and the deep layer of the postsynaptic density.
Échafaudage de la couche profonde (SHANK: Scaffold of the deep layer (SHANK1 to SHANK3). It binds GKAP, Homer and cortactin, and so links the receptors to the actin of the spine. Loss of one copy of SHANK3 (22q13.3 deletion) causes Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
Tétramères qui pontent Shank, les récept: Tetramers that bridge Shank, mGluR1/5 receptors and the IP3 receptors of the reticulum. The short form Homer1a, induced by activity, undoes these bridges.
Kinase en dodécamère (deux anneaux de si: A dodecameric kinase (two rings of six subunits, ≈ 20 nm), the most abundant protein of the postsynaptic density. Activated by Ca²⁺/calmodulin, it autophosphorylates on Thr286 and stays active after the calcium signal has ended; it binds GluN2B and promotes the addition of AMPA receptors: long-term potentiation (Lisman 2012). Variants of CAMK2A and CAMK2B cause intellectual disability.
Réseau de filaments branchés (Arp2/3), r: A network of branched filaments (Arp2/3), renewed in less than a minute. It gives the spine its shape: the head enlarges during potentiation and shrinks during depression.
Empilement de citernes de réticulum liss: A stack of smooth reticulum cisternae, organised by synaptopodin, found in a minority of spines, the largest ones. A Ca²⁺ store and a relay for local protein trafficking.
Une seule chaîne (gène SCN8A) de quatre: A single chain (gene SCN8A) of four domains with six transmembrane segments each; the charged S4 segments are the voltage sensors. It opens in less than a millisecond, then inactivates by itself: the IFM motif of the III–IV loop plugs the pore (orange bead, cytosolic side). The Nav1.6 channels of the distal initial segment trigger the action potential; the proximal Nav1.2 (SCN2A) channels carry it back towards the soma (Hu 2009). SCN1A, SCN2A and SCN8A are epileptic encephalopathy genes.
Tétramères dépendants du voltage. Les Kv: Voltage-gated tetramers. Kv7.2/7.3 (KCNQ2, KCNQ3; green) carry the M current, a brake that acts below threshold; Kv1.1/1.2 (KCNA1, KCNA2; blue-green), in the distal initial segment, quickly repolarise the action potential. Their selectivity filter lets K⁺ through but not Na⁺. KCNQ2 variants cause neonatal epilepsies.
Elle sort 3 Na⁺ et fait entrer 2 K⁺ par: It exports 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ per ATP: it maintains the gradients that each action potential barely dents, and uses a large share of the brain's ATP. The neuronal α3 isoform is encoded by ATP1A3 (alternating hemiplegia of childhood). Its mechanism is detailed in the ⚗ chemical reactions of the cytosol.
Dimères à deux domaines pore (TREK, TASK: Dimers with two pore domains each (TREK, TASK; KCNK genes), open at rest. Through them the membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺, which sets the resting potential near −70 mV.
L'ankyrine G (gène ANK3) est le maître d: Ankyrin G (gene ANK3) is the master organiser of the initial segment: it anchors Nav and Kv7 channels there and links them to βIV spectrin (SPTBN4), stretched between actin rings spaced ≈ 190 nm apart.
Au repos : une membrane sous tension: At rest: a membrane under tension
Voici une synapse excitatrice que reçoit: Here is an excitatory synapse received by our neuron. Above, the bouton of an afferent axon, filled with glutamate vesicles; below, the spine of our dendrite; between them, a 20 nm cleft; on the side, an astrocyte process. At rest, the inside of the neuron sits at −70 mV relative to the outside. A stimulus is about to arrive along the afferent axon.
Le potentiel de repos (≈ −70 mV) tient à: The resting potential (≈ −70 mV) results from gradients maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP) and from a permeability dominated by K⁺ (K2P leak channels): the membrane sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential (≈ −90 mV), raised a little by a small Na⁺ leak (Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation). Typical concentrations: K⁺ 140 mM inside, 4 mM outside; Na⁺ 12 mM inside, 145 mM outside; free Ca²⁺ 0.1 µM inside, 1.2 mM outside.
Quel ion domine la perméabilité de la me: Which ion dominates membrane permeability at rest?
Le potentiel d'action envahit le bouton: The action potential invades the bouton
Zone active du bouton afférent: Active zone of the afferent bouton
Le potentiel d'action de l'axone afféren: The action potential of the afferent axon depolarises the bouton. The Cav2.1 calcium channels (magenta), clustered 20–30 nm from the docked vesicles (yellow), open: Ca²⁺ (orange), ten thousand times more concentrated outside than inside, rushes in and within a fraction of a millisecond forms a highly concentrated nanodomain around each vesicle.
Les Cav2.1 (type P/Q, gène CACNA1A) sont: Cav2.1 channels (P/Q type, gene CACNA1A) are tethered to the active zone by RIM and RIM-BP, which places them a few tens of nanometres from the Ca²⁺ sensor. They let Ca²⁺ in mostly during the repolarisation of the action potential, when the driving force becomes strong again. In the nanodomain, Ca²⁺ reaches tens of µM for less than a millisecond. Release varies as roughly the 4th power of the Ca²⁺ concentration: a small change in Ca²⁺ entry greatly changes the probability of release.
Pourquoi les canaux Cav2.1 sont-ils atta: Why are Cav2.1 channels tethered so close to the docked vesicles?
Le Ca²⁺ n'atteint des dizaines de µM qu': Ca²⁺ reaches tens of µM only within a few tens of nm of the channel
Pour laisser passer le glutamate vers la: To let glutamate through to the cleft
Parce qu'ils fournissent l'ATP de la fus: Because they supply the ATP for fusion
Le Ca²⁺ se lie à la synaptotagmine-1 (or: Ca²⁺ binds to synaptotagmin-1 (orange) on the docked vesicle. The SNARE complex (red), already half zippered, closes like a zip and forces the two membranes to fuse: a pore opens and 1,500 to 2,000 glutamate molecules pour into the cleft. All of this takes less than a millisecond.
La synaptotagmine-1 fixe le Ca²⁺ par ses: Synaptotagmin-1 binds Ca²⁺ through its C2A and C2B domains, plunges into the plasma membrane and releases the complexin brake. The zippering of the four helices of the SNARE complex (syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 on the membrane, synaptobrevin-2 on the vesicle), prepared by Munc18-1 and Munc13-1, supplies the energy for fusion (Südhof 2013). An action potential releases a vesicle only with a certain probability: transmission is quantal and probabilistic. Botulinum and tetanus toxins are proteases that cleave SNAREs.
Qu'est-ce qui fournit l'énergie de la fu: What supplies the energy for membrane fusion?
L'enroulement du complexe SNARE: The zippering of the SNARE complex
Le gradient de protons de la vésicule: The proton gradient of the vesicle
Le glutamate (blanc-vert) traverse la fe: Glutamate (pale green) crosses the cleft in a few microseconds and binds to the AMPA receptors (blue) lying just opposite the release site. Their channel opens in less than a millisecond: Na⁺ (yellow) flows in and the spine membrane depolarises by a few millivolts. This is the excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP). The NMDA receptor (pink) remains plugged by a Mg²⁺ ion.
Le récepteur AMPA est un tétramère (GluA: The AMPA receptor is a low-affinity tetramer (GluA1 to GluA4): only receptors close to the fusion pore see enough glutamate (peak ≈ 1 mM, gone within ≈ 1 ms; Clements 1992). Hence the importance of nanocolumns: the receptor nanodomains, held by PSD-95 and TARPs, are aligned with the release sites marked by RIM (Tang 2016). The channel passes Na⁺ and K⁺ (reversal potential ≈ 0 mV); the edited GluA2 subunit (Q/R) makes it impermeable to Ca²⁺. The current lasts only a few milliseconds (deactivation, desensitisation).
Pourquoi l'alignement des récepteurs AMP: Why does the alignment of AMPA receptors with the release site matter?
Leur affinité est faible : seul le gluta: Their affinity is low: only very concentrated glutamate, near the pore, opens them
Parce qu'ils doivent toucher la vésicule: Because they must touch the vesicle
Le récepteur NMDA (rose) a lui aussi fix: The NMDA receptor (pink) has also bound glutamate, but its pore is plugged by a Mg²⁺ ion (bright pink) as long as the membrane is close to rest. If the spine is strongly depolarised at the same moment — several synapses active together, or an action potential travelling back up the dendrite — the Mg²⁺ is expelled and Ca²⁺ (orange) enters. This Ca²⁺ activates CaMKII: the synapse will be strengthened.
Le récepteur NMDA (2 GluN1 + 2 GluN2) ex: The NMDA receptor (2 GluN1 + 2 GluN2) requires three conditions: glutamate, a co-agonist (glycine or D-serine) and a depolarisation that relieves the Mg²⁺ block. It is slow (tens to hundreds of ms) and highly permeable to Ca²⁺. Ca²⁺/calmodulin activates CaMKII, whose autophosphorylation on Thr286 prolongs its activity; it binds GluN2B and promotes the addition of AMPA receptors to the postsynaptic density: this is long-term potentiation (Lisman 2012). The spine, isolated by its neck, confines this calcium signal to the active synapse.
Qu'est-ce qui lève le bloc du récepteur: What relieves the Mg²⁺ block of the NMDA receptor?
La fixation d'une seconde molécule de gl: Binding of a second glutamate molecule
Fin du signal : capture du glutamate, re: End of the signal: glutamate uptake, recycling
Bord de la fente et astrocyte: Edge of the cleft and astrocyte
Le signal doit s'arrêter vite. Le glutam: The signal must stop quickly. Glutamate diffuses out of the cleft; the GLT-1 transporters (green) of the astrocyte process take it up, the astrocyte converts it into glutamine and returns it to the neuron. On the bouton side, the vesicle membrane is retrieved by endocytosis and a new vesicle docks at the vacated site.
GLT-1 (EAAT2) fait entrer un glutamate a: GLT-1 (EAAT2) brings in one glutamate with 3 Na⁺ and 1 H⁺ and exports 1 K⁺: enough energy to keep extracellular glutamate below one micromolar. One transport cycle takes tens of milliseconds; it is the sheer number of transporters (thousands per µm²) that traps glutamate quickly. In the astrocyte, glutamine synthetase converts it into glutamine (the glutamate–glutamine cycle). In the bouton, endocytosis (clathrin, dynamin; an ultrafast pathway also exists) regenerates vesicles, the V-ATPase acidifies them and VGLUT1 fills them. NSF and α-SNAP take the SNARE complexes apart using ATP.
Quelle énergie GLT-1 utilise-t-il pour c: What energy does GLT-1 use to take up glutamate?
Le gradient de Na⁺ (avec H⁺ et K⁺): The Na⁺ gradient (with H⁺ and K⁺)
Le gradient de protons des vésicules: The proton gradient of the vesicles
Le PPSE se propage dans la dendrite: The EPSP spreads along the dendrite
Le courant entré dans l'épine s'écoule d: The current that entered the spine flows into the dendrite and reaches the soma without being amplified: like water in a leaky hose, the signal fades and spreads out on the way. An EPSP of several millivolts in the spine is worth only a few tenths of a millivolt at the soma. Meanwhile, other synapses fire (flashes): their EPSPs add up.
La dendrite se comporte comme un câble :: The dendrite behaves like a cable: axial resistance, membrane resistance and membrane capacitance set a length constant (hundreds of µm) and a time constant (tens of ms) that filter the signal. Spatial summation: distinct synapses active together; temporal summation: one synapse active at high frequency. The dendrite is not merely passive: its HCN (Ih current), Kv4 and Nav channels shape integration, and distal synapses have a larger conductance, which partly offsets their distance (Magee 2000). On the order of tens to a hundred synapses must be active together to reach threshold.
Que devient l'amplitude d'un PPSE entre: What happens to the amplitude of an EPSP between the spine and the soma?
Elle reste constante, comme celle d'un p: It stays constant, like that of an action potential
Elle augmente à chaque embranchement: It increases at every branch point
Sommation au soma : excitation contre in: Summation at the soma: excitation versus inhibition
Le soma additionne à chaque instant ce q: At every instant the soma adds up whatever arrives from the dendrites. EPSPs (yellow) raise the potential; inhibitory GABAergic synapses on the soma (green flash) open Cl⁻ channels that hold it near rest. If the sum reaches threshold, ≈ −55 mV, the neuron fires; otherwise nothing leaves. On the oscilloscope, each step is a volley of synapses active together.
Le récepteur GABA-A est un canal à Cl⁻ p: The GABA-A receptor is a pentameric Cl⁻ channel. In the mature neuron, the KCC2 transporter keeps internal Cl⁻ low, so that its equilibrium potential is close to rest: inhibition acts mainly as a short circuit (“shunt”) that reduces the effect of neighbouring EPSPs. Placed on the soma, just before the axon initial segment, it holds a veto. The oscilloscope shows stepwise summation, an inhibitory potential that delays it, then the crossing of threshold.
Pourquoi une synapse inhibitrice posée s: Why is an inhibitory synapse on the soma so effective?
Elle agit juste avant la zone de déclenc: It acts just before the trigger zone and short-circuits the EPSPs
Elle libère plus de neurotransmetteur qu: It releases more neurotransmitter than a dendritic synapse
Elle bloque directement les canaux Nav d: It directly blocks the Nav channels of the axon
Voici la membrane du segment initial de: This is the membrane of the axon initial segment, seen in section: the outside is at the top, the cytosol at the bottom. Nav1.6 sodium channels (red) are very dense here and open for a smaller depolarisation than elsewhere. As soon as a few open, Na⁺ (yellow) flows in, depolarises further and opens the neighbouring channels: the reaction runs away. The action potential is born here.
Chaque canal Nav est une seule chaîne de: Each Nav channel is a single chain of four domains; its charged S4 segments are the voltage sensors. The Nav1.6 channels (SCN8A) of the distal initial segment have a low activation threshold and trigger the action potential; the proximal Nav1.2 channels (SCN2A) carry its backpropagation towards the soma and dendrites (Hu 2009). Ankyrin G (ANK3) anchors Nav and Kv7 to βIV spectrin. Kv7 channels (KCNQ2/3, M current) restrain excitability below threshold. The length and position of the initial segment adjust to the neuron's activity (Kole and Stuart 2012).
Pourquoi le potentiel d'action naît-il a: Why does the action potential start at the initial segment rather than at the soma?
Les canaux Nav y sont très denses et leu: Nav channels are very dense there and their threshold is low
Le potentiel d'action, phase par phase: The action potential, phase by phase
Suivez le curseur de l'oscilloscope. Mon: Follow the oscilloscope cursor. Upstroke: Nav channels open, Na⁺ flows in, the potential jumps from −55 to ≈ +30 mV in less than a millisecond. Peak: Nav channels inactivate by themselves (orange plug). Downstroke: the slower K⁺ channels (green) open; K⁺ (violet) flows out and brings the potential back to slightly below rest. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (gold) then restores the gradients.
L'inactivation rapide vient du motif IFM: Fast inactivation comes from the IFM motif of the loop between domains III and IV, which plugs the pore within ≈ 1 ms; until it is removed by the return to rest, the channel cannot reopen: this is the absolute refractory period (≈ 1 to 2 ms), followed by a relative refractory period due to Kv channels that are still open. The action potential is all-or-none: its amplitude does not depend on the stimulus; information is carried by the rate and timing of firing. Each action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the ions: concentrations barely change.
Qu'est-ce qui empêche un canal Nav de se: What prevents a Nav channel from reopening immediately?
Son inactivation, levée seulement après: Its inactivation, removed only after the return to rest
Le Na⁺ entré dépolarise la portion de me: The Na⁺ that entered depolarises the next stretch of membrane, which opens in turn: the action potential regenerates step by step, without fading. Behind the front (yellow), the membrane is refractory (violet): the wave cannot turn back. In this thin, unmyelinated collateral it travels at a few tenths of a metre per second.
Dans un axone sans myéline, la vitesse c: In an unmyelinated axon, velocity grows as the square root of the diameter (≈ 0.2 to 0.5 m/s for hippocampal collaterals; our 22 µm are covered in less than 0.1 ms). Myelin (not drawn here) insulates the axon and lowers its capacitance: the action potential then jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next — saltatory conduction, up to ≈ 100 m/s — and Nav1.6 channels cluster at the nodes. The action potential also travels back towards the soma and dendrites: this backpropagation tells the synapses that the neuron has fired.
Pourquoi le potentiel d'action ne repart: Why does the action potential not travel backwards?
La membrane qu'il vient de quitter est r: The membrane it has just left is refractory
Les canaux Nav ne laissent passer le Na⁺: Nav channels let Na⁺ through in one direction only
Au bouton : le message passe au neurone: At the bouton: the message passes to the next neuron
Le potentiel d'action atteint notre bout: The action potential reaches our bouton. The opening sequence plays again, but now it is our neuron that speaks: Ca²⁺ through Cav2.1, fusion of a vesicle, glutamate in the cleft, opening of the AMPA receptors on the spine of the next neuron. Less than a millisecond elapses between the arrival of the action potential and the postsynaptic response.
Le signal électrique est converti en sig: The electrical signal is converted into a chemical signal, then back into an electrical one: the chemical synapse is one-way, tunable (release probability, number of receptors) and plastic in the short term (facilitation by residual Ca²⁺, depression by depletion of ready vesicles). The synaptic delay is due mainly to the opening of Ca²⁺ channels and to fusion; crossing the cleft takes only microseconds. A hippocampal bouton has on average one active zone of ≈ 0.04 µm², about ten docked vesicles and ≈ 200 vesicles in all (Schikorski and Stevens 1997).
D'où vient l'essentiel du délai synaptiq: Where does most of the synaptic delay come from?
De l'ouverture des canaux Ca²⁺ et de la: From the opening of Ca²⁺ channels and the fusion of the vesicle
De la diffusion du glutamate à travers l: From the diffusion of glutamate across the cleft
Du trajet du potentiel d'action dans le: From the travel of the action potential within the bouton
Montée : Nav ouverts, le Na⁺ entre: Upstroke: Nav open, Na⁺ flows in
Descente : Nav inactivés, Kv ouverts, le: Downstroke: Nav inactivated, Kv open, K⁺ flows out
Retour au repos : la pompe Na⁺/K⁺ travai: Back to rest: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump at work
Vm · épine du neurone suivant: Vm · spine of the next neuron
En quelques millisecondes : potentiel d': In a few milliseconds: afferent action potential, Ca²⁺ entry, glutamate, EPSP in the spine, summation in the dendrite and soma, threshold at the initial segment, action potential, conduction, release onto the next neuron. Activity also leaves a trace in the nucleus: the Ca²⁺ that entered through NMDA receptors and L-type Cav channels activates CREB and SRF, and the FOS gene — the one you can transcribe in this neuron — switches on within minutes. Animation slowed more than a thousandfold; numbers of molecules reduced; schematic geometries and traces.
Vous êtes au bord de la fente synaptique: You are at the edge of the synaptic cleft: move forward, the ship shrinks to slip in. Tap a molecule to identify it.
Un stimulus arrive par une synapse de la: A stimulus arrives at a synapse of the apical dendrite. Follow the signal step by step: glutamate release, postsynaptic potential, summation, threshold at the initial segment, action potential, conduction along the axon, down to the synapse that our bouton forms on the next neuron. At each step, an oscilloscope traces the membrane potential. Rotate the scene, zoom in.
Fine expansion d'un astrocyte accolée au: A fine astrocyte process pressed against the edge of the synapse (the “tripartite” synapse); in the hippocampus, more than half of the synapses have one. It takes up the glutamate and K⁺ that escape from the cleft, and returns glutamine to the neuron. Its contribution to D-serine, a co-agonist of NMDA receptors, is still debated.
